title: Autonomous Code Migration for Quantum Programming Languages: A Case Study with QED-C Benchmarks
authors: W. Michael Brown, Thien Nguyen, Avimita Chatterjee, Thomas Lubinski
abstract: Quantum programming requires concepts and intuition that differ substantially from those used in traditional programming languages. Multiple quantum programming frameworks address these requirements through different abstractions and execution models, creating tradeoffs in programmability, portability, and performance. Because quantum software is less prevalent in the training data available to large language models, autonomous coding agents might be expected to face additional challenges when working with these frameworks. We present a case study in autonomous migration of the QED-C Application-Oriented Benchmarks from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. Opus, GPT, and Gemini models were each tasked with porting thirteen benchmark methods spanning foundational algorithms, amplitude estimation, Monte Carlo methods, variational optimization, linear-system solving, and factoring. In all cases, the models were able to generate satisfactory ports with little direct coding help and there was a drastic reduction in the time required compared to a human engineer. However, in all cases, the agents resorted to shortcuts when implementation challenges surfaced and multiple prompts were required to force appropriate coding directions. Assessment of the generated implementations showed that no single model consistently produced the best port across all benchmarks, indicating that multi-agent ensemble strategies could mitigate challenges associated with quantum software. The effort resulted in publicly available, near-complete CUDA-Q support in the QED-C benchmarks along with model-generated skills designed to improve agent performance when implementing CUDA-Q applications. When tested on an unseen benchmark, these skills reduced the required model turns by up to 85% and token usage by up to 96%. We conclude by distilling lessons from the case study.
summary: This paper details a case study on using large language models to autonomously migrate quantum code benchmarks from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. The research demonstrates that while LLMs can significantly reduce human effort in this complex task, the process is improved by distilling reusable 'skills' from the initial migrations. This work advances the state-of-the-art in automated quantum software engineering.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of autonomously migrating quantum algorithms and benchmarks from one programming framework (Qiskit) to another (CUDA-Q). This is necessary because quantum software requires specialized abstractions that differ significantly from traditional programming languages.
main_result: LLMs successfully generated satisfactory code ports with significantly reduced human effort, and distilling 'skills' from these migrations improved agent performance on unseen benchmarks by reducing required model turns by up to 85%.
method: The authors used large language models (Opus, GPT, Gemini) as agents to port thirteen QED-C benchmark methods from Qiskit to CUDA-Q. They then tested knowledge transfer by creating and applying reusable 'skills' derived from these initial migrations.
model_or_system: The work operates on quantum computing platforms, specifically comparing the Qiskit and CUDA-Q frameworks. The benchmarks cover diverse quantum algorithms including amplitude estimation, variational optimization, and factoring.
key_observables: Model turns required for porting, token usage, fidelity of generated code, and the percentage reduction in model turns/tokens when using distilled skills.
important_parameters: The benchmark suite includes 13 methods spanning foundational algorithms, Monte Carlo, and optimization tasks.
main_assumptions: The study assumes that algorithmic intent can be preserved across framework abstractions, though it notes that this is not guaranteed and that agents can use 'shortcuts.'
figures_summary: The notes reference a figure detailing the two pathways: autonomous migration (Pathway 1) and knowledge transfer using reusable skills (Pathway 2). Tables quantify the percentage reduction in model turns and token count achieved by these skills.
paper_structure: The paper follows a case study structure: first, performing the autonomous migration of the QED-C benchmarks across multiple LLMs; second, analyzing the resulting challenges and inconsistencies; and finally, developing and testing a knowledge-transfer mechanism using 'skills' to improve future agent performance.
why_interesting: While the focus is on software engineering rather than fundamental physics, the successful automation of complex quantum algorithm implementation across platforms is crucial for realizing quantum hardware, directly impacting the practical application of quantum information science.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the autonomous code-migration and knowledge-transfer methodology. In Pathway 1, three coding agents independently migrate the 13 QED-C benchmark methods from Qiskit to CUDA-Q under isolated contexts. The resulting implementations are validated and characterized using fidelity, migration-effort, code-size, and gate-structure measures, followed by cross-agent assessment and ensemble consolidation. In Pathway 2, experience from the first 11 benchmark migrations is distilled into model-generated skills and evaluated on the held-out Shor’s Methods 1 and 2 under clean contexts, including both self-use and cross-model skill transfer.
